::: {.lead}
Today you work like in a lab: you do four experiments in PowerPoint on a
short talk and record what you see. Do each experiment when your teacher
shows it. After each step, write your result in its box. At the end, copy
your key results into the table.
:::

## Before you start

- **You need:** a computer with PowerPoint (the desktop app, or PowerPoint
  on the web at `office.com`).
- **Time:** about 40 minutes for the four experiments.
- **Check:** the results are at the end of this worksheet. Look only after
  you try. On the interactive lesson, every step has a check that answers
  at once.

{{< start-files >}}

## Experiment 1 · Slides and layouts

**Aim:** see the parts of the window, choose a layout, and start the slide
show. *(Lesson notes 8.1 · about 10 minutes)*

1. Open `talk-start.pptx` (click **Enable Editing** if you see it). Count
   the thumbnails on the left. Click slide 1 and open **Home › Layout**:
   the layout of the slide is marked.

   {{< record "Slides: … ; slide 1 has the layout …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **3 slides.** Slide 1 has the layout **Title Slide**: a big title and a
   subtitle.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   Which layout has slide 1?

   - [x] Title Slide

     Why: A big title and a subtitle. The talk has 3 slides.

   - [ ] Two Content

     Why: Two content boxes side by side: that is the new slide of step 2.

   - [ ] Blank

     Why: Slide 1 has a title and a subtitle.
   :::

2. Click slide 3. Choose **Home › New Slide › Two Content**. Type the title
   *Before and after*.

   {{< record "How many placeholders does the new slide have?" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **3 placeholders**: the title and two content boxes side by side. You
   click in a placeholder and type: no text boxes of your own.
   :::

   ::: {.fill answer="3" unit="placeholders" hint="Count the title and the boxes side by side."}
   How many placeholders does the new **Two Content** slide have?

   Why: The title and two content boxes side by side. You click in a placeholder and type: no text boxes of your own.
   :::

3. Press **F5** and click through the talk. Then press **Esc**.

   {{< record "F5 starts the show from slide … ; Esc …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   F5 starts the show from **slide 1**, on the full screen. **Esc** stops
   the show and goes back to the normal view.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   You press **F5**. Where does the show start?

   - [x] at slide 1, on the full screen

     Why: F5 starts from the beginning. Esc stops the show and goes back to the normal view.

   - [ ] at the slide that you clicked

     Why: F5 always starts at slide 1.

   - [ ] in a small window next to the slides

     Why: The show fills the whole screen.
   :::

## Experiment 2 · A theme

**Aim:** give the whole talk one look, and keep a strong contrast.
*(Lesson notes 8.2 · about 8 minutes)*

1. On the **Design** tab, click a theme that you like.

   {{< record "My theme; which slides changed?" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **All four slides** change their colours, fonts and background at once:
   a theme gives the whole talk one look.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   You click a theme. Which slides change?

   - [x] all four slides, at once

     Why: A theme gives the whole talk one look: colours, fonts and background.

   - [ ] only the slide that you clicked

     Why: A theme is for the whole talk.

   - [ ] only slide 1

     Why: Every slide gets the theme.
   :::

2. Click two **Variants** (Design › Variants), one after the other.

   {{< record "What does a variant change?" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   The **colours** change, but the design stays the same theme. Keep the
   variant that you like best.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   What does a variant change?

   - [x] the colours: the design stays the same theme

     Why: A variant is a version of the theme. Keep the one that you like best.

   - [ ] the whole theme

     Why: The design stays: only the colours change.

   - [ ] the text of the slides

     Why: The Design tab changes the look, never the words.
   :::

3. Go to slide 3. Stand two metres away from your screen and read it.

   {{< record "Can I read every word? Dark on light, or light on dark?" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A good result: you can read every word, because the contrast is strong
   (dark text on a light background, or light text on a dark one). If you
   cannot, choose another variant.
   :::

   ::: {.sort}
   Easy or hard to read from two metres? Sort the slides.

   Easy to read: a strong contrast
   :   dark text on a light background

       Why: Dark on light: a strong contrast.

   :   light text on a dark background

       Why: Light on dark works too.

   Hard to read: a weak contrast
   :   light grey text on a white background

       Why: Light on light: choose another variant.

   :   dark blue text on a black background

       Why: Dark on dark: choose another variant.
   :::

## Experiment 3 · Few words and notes

**Aim:** keep few words on the slide, and put the rest in the notes.
*(Lesson notes 8.3 · about 12 minutes)*

1. Click slide 2, *Small changes at home*. Count its points, and the words
   of its longest point.

   {{< record "Points: … ; the longest has … words" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **6 points**, and the longest has **18 words**. That is too much text:
   nobody reads it from the back of the room.
   :::

   ::: {.fill answer="6" unit="points" hint="Count the lines that start with a bullet."}
   How many points has slide 2?

   Why: 6 points, and the longest has 18 words. That is too much text: nobody reads it from the back of the room.
   :::

2. Click in the text, press **Ctrl + A** and **Ctrl + C**. Open **View ›
   Notes** and paste the text into the notes pane under the slide.

   {{< record "Where is the text now?" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   The long text is **on the slide and in the notes pane**. The notes keep
   the details that you will say.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   Where is the long text now?

   - [x] on the slide and in the notes pane

     Why: You copied it. The notes keep the details that you will say.

   - [ ] only in the notes pane

     Why: Ctrl + C copies: the text is still on the slide.

   - [ ] on a new slide

     Why: You pasted it into the notes under the slide.
   :::

3. Now make the slide short: keep **3 to 5 points**, each with **8 words or
   fewer**.

   {{< record "My shortest point" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A good result, for example: "Close the tap while you brush", "Fix a
   dripping tap", "Take a short shower", "Use a bucket for the car". The
   details stay in the notes. In the slide show, only you see the notes
   (Presenter View).
   :::

   ::: {.sort}
   A good point for the slide, or too long? Sort them.

   Good: 8 words or fewer
   :   Close the tap while you brush

       Why: 6 words: easy to read from the back.

   :   Fix a dripping tap

       Why: 4 words.

   :   Take a short shower

       Why: 4 words.

   Too long: keep it in the notes
   :   When you brush your teeth, please remember to close the tap so the water does not run

       Why: 17 words: say it, and show only a few key words.
   :::

## Experiment 4 · A transition and an animation

**Aim:** add one quiet transition to every slide, and show points one by
one. *(Lesson notes 8.4 · about 10 minutes)*

1. On the **Transitions** tab, choose **Fade**. Set the **Duration** to
   **00.70** and click **Apply To All**. Look at the thumbnails.

   {{< record "What appears next to every thumbnail?" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A **small star** appears next to every thumbnail: each slide now has a
   transition. Apply To All gave every slide the same quiet Fade.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   After **Apply To All**, what appears next to every thumbnail?

   - [x] a small star

     Why: Each slide now has a transition: the same quiet Fade.

   - [ ] a number

     Why: Numbers mark the animations on a slide (step 2).

   - [ ] nothing

     Why: The star shows that the slide has a transition.
   :::

2. Click slide 3, *What we do at the office*. Click in its three points and
   choose **Animations › Appear**. Then choose **Effect Options › By
   Paragraph**.

   {{< record "Which numbers appear next to the points?" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **1, 2 and 3**, one next to each point: the order of the clicks in the
   slide show.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   After **By Paragraph**, what appears next to the three points?

   - [x] 1, 2 and 3: one number next to each point

     Why: The numbers are the order of the clicks in the slide show.

   - [ ] 1 next to all three points

     Why: All three would come on one click; By Paragraph gives each point its own click.

   - [ ] a star next to each point

     Why: The star is for a transition, next to the thumbnail.
   :::

3. Press **F5** and click until the end of slide 3. Then press **Esc**.

   {{< record "On slide 3, what comes with each click?" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   The slides fade into each other in less than a second. On slide 3 the
   title comes first, then **one point on each click**. Few, quiet effects
   keep the eyes on your message.
   :::

   ::: {.order}
   In the slide show, put what comes on slide 3 in order.

   1. The slide fades in, with its title.
   2. Click: the first point appears.
   3. Click: the second point appears.
   4. Click: the third point appears.

   Why: The title comes first, then one point on each click. Few, quiet effects keep the eyes on your message.
   :::
